title: Suppression of sleep syncope and vagally-mediated asystole by norepinephrine transporter inhibitor
case_prompt:
A 70-year-old patient presented with a history of recurrent syncope that began in 2019. Over the first year, the patient experienced 11 syncopal episodes and up to 9 presyncopal episodes per day. The daytime events typically occurred while the patient was sitting quietly and were preceded by lightheadedness, nausea, warmth, and diaphoresis lasting several minutes. Episodes often culminated in loss of consciousness for up to 60 seconds upon standing, after which the patient regained consciousness pale and diaphoretic.

In April 2020, the patient described 3 additional spells that differed from the previous pattern: in 3 instances the patient fainted while sitting quietly, and in 1 instance the patient was supine in bed at night when a sudden sensation of warmth and presyncope was followed by syncope. These nocturnal events were witnessed and associated with disturbed breathing and brief unresponsiveness.

The patient’s medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, and prior smoking; the only medication was irbesartan 150 mg daily. On examination, blood pressure was 150/95 mm Hg; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. A baseline ECG, transthoracic echocardiogram, ambulatory blood pressure monitor, and 24-hour Holter monitor were all normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cardiac arrhythmia was considered because of high syncope recurrence and nocturnal spells but was deemed unlikely — “the baseline electrocardiogram, transthoracic echocardiogram, ambulatory blood pressure monitor, and 24-hour Holter monitors were all normal.”  
2. Vasovagal syncope was considered based on the typical daytime prodrome of lightheadedness, nausea, warmth, and sweatiness during quiet sitting — “The events usually occurred while the patient was sitting quietly, with a prodrome of lightheadedness, nausea, warmth, and sweatiness…”  
3. A sleep syncope variant was favored for nocturnal spells occurring supine with vagal symptoms — “in 1 spell the patient was supine in bed at night…There was a sudden onset of an episode of presyncope with a sensation of warmth, followed by syncope.”  
4. Definitive confirmation of vasovagal sleep syncope came from ILR monitoring showing prolonged asystole with vagal characteristics — “The ILR recorded a 35.6-second asystolic pause preceded by sinus slowing and followed by sinus bradycardia…fits the European Heart Rhythm Association…diagnostic criteria for vagally mediated asystole.”
